cm6_clarity_of_research_objectives.reason: The research objectives are clearly stated. The study explicitly tests the hypothesis that social behavioral problems in children with ASD are attributed to deviations in between-network rsFC from the established norm. The authors specify their three main objectives: (1) generate normative trajectories of between-network rsFC, (2) examine associations between rsFC deviations and distinct domains of social behaviors, and (3) examine whether executive function mediates the association between atypical rsFC and social behaviors. The application purpose of normative modeling is clearly stated as enabling precision diagnosis and treatment in ASD by identifying individual-level deviations.
cm6_clarity_of_research_objectives.supporting_text: We posit that social behavioral problems observed in children with ASD are attributed to deviations in between-network rsFC from the established norm. To test this hypothesis, we used data from the ABIDE consortium (Di Martino et al., 2014). We focused exclusively on males due to the increased prevalence of ASD in males (Werling and Geschwind, 2013) providing us with a greater study sample size and the sex differences observed in neurodevelopmental trajectories (Bethlehem et al., 2022) that would make it inadvisable to study males and females as one cohort. We first generated normative trajectories of between-network rsFC from 321 typically developing males between ages 5 and 14 years using generalized additive models. We then aligned these normative charts to rsFC measures of 418 males with ASD to quantify between-network rsFC deviations at the level of individual participants. Next, we examined the associations between rsFC deviations and distinct domains of social behaviors using sparse canonical correlation analysis.

common_part.cm7_additional_comments: This study builds normative models of between-network resting-state functional connectivity using data from the ABIDE consortium. The study focuses exclusively on males aged 5-14 years and examines how functional connectivity deviations relate to social behavioral problems and executive functioning in ASD. The study employs Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) for normative modeling and uses sparse canonical correlation analysis to identify relationships between FC deviations and social behavior subscales.

The preprocessing software is clearly specified: CONN Toolbox v20b with SPM12. Each preprocessing step is detailed: (1) realignment with SPM12 realign & unwarp procedure, (2) slice-timing correction using SPM12 STC procedure, (3) identification of outlier volumes (framewise displacement >0.9mm or global BOLD signal changes >5 SD), (4) normalization into standard MNI space and segmentation using SPM12 unified segmentation and normalization procedure, (5) spatial smoothing with 6mm FWHM Gaussian kernel, (6) exclusion of first four scans, and (7) denoising with OLS regression and band-pass filtering (0.008-0.09 Hz). nm6_details_of_data_preprocessing.supporting_text: Resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) data was processed as previously described (Chan et al., 2024), with the default pre-processing and de-noising pipelines using the CONN Toolbox v20b (Whitfield-Gabrieli and Nieto-Castanon, 2012). Scans underwent realignment with SPM12 realign & unwarp procedure (Andersson et al., 2001). Temporal misalignment between different slices of the functional data was corrected using SPM12 slice-timing correction (STC) procedure (Henson et al., 1999). Scan volumes with framewise displacement above 0.9 mm or global BOLD signal changes above 5 standard deviations were identified as potential outliers. Functional and anatomical data were normalized into standard MNI space and segmented into grey matter, white matter, and CSF tissue classes using SPM12 unified segmentation and normalization procedure (Ashburner and Friston, 2005). Functional data was smoothed using spatial convolution with a Gaussian kernel of 6 mm full width half maximum (FWHM), and the first four scans excluded to allow for magnetic field saturation. For denoising, BOLD signal variance over time explained by nuisance variables, including scan volumes identified as potential outliers, was removed from the data using Ordinary Least Squares regression, and the BOLD time series were band-pass filtered to preserve only frequencies between 0.008 and 0.09 Hz.

Functional data was smoothed using spatial convolution with a Gaussian kernel of 6 mm full width half maximum (FWHM), and the first four scans excluded to allow for magnetic field saturation. cr6_validity_of_outcome_measures.reason: The study clearly defines and validates its outcome measures. Outcomes are pre-specified and operationally defined: Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS) for social behavior deficits and Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF) for executive function. The SRS is described as a 65-item questionnaire with 5 subscales (social awareness, cognition, motivation, communication, mannerisms) scored on a 4-point Likert scale, with higher scores indicating greater problems. The BRIEF is an 86-item questionnaire with 8 clinical subscales and a Global Executive Composite (GEC) score, scored on a 3-point Likert scale. Both instruments are validated and standard measures widely used in ASD research. Reliability is implicitly supported by using established, published instruments. T-scores are used for both SRS and BRIEF, which are normalized for age and sex. Implementation is consistent across participants as all use the same validated instruments. The study acknowledges a limitation regarding unmeasured confounders in mediation analysis.
cr6_validity_of_outcome_measures.supporting_text: The SRS (Constantino and Gruber, 2005) was used to measure parent-rated deficits in social behavior. The questionnaire consists of 65 items that are grouped into five subscales; (1) social awareness, (2) social cognition, (3) social motivation, (4) social communication, and (5) mannerisms (also known as restricted interests and repetitive behavior). Items are scored on a 4-point Likert scale (1 = Not true, 4 = Almost always true), with a higher score indicating greater problems with social behavior associated with ASD. The T-scores for SRS total and all 5 subscales were used in our analyses, as they are normalized for age and sex. The BRIEF (Gioia et al., 2000) is an 86-item questionnaire used to assess executive function performance in participants aged between 5 and 18 years. Each item is scored on a 3-point Likert scale. Higher scores indicate poorer executive function performance. BRIEF consists of eight clinical subscales, (1) Inhibit, (2) Shift (Cognitive Flexibility), (3) Emotional Control, (4) Initiate, (5) Working Memory, (6) Plan/Organize, (7) Organization of Materials and (8) Monitor. The General Executive Composite (GEC) score is the sum of these 8 clinical subscale scores. Raw scores were linearly transformed to obtain T-scores, which were used in our analyses.

cr7_handling_of_confounding_variables.reason: The study comprehensively handles confounding variables at multiple levels. Basic confounders (age and sex) are addressed: age is included as a predictor in normative models with smoothing function for non-linear trajectories, and the study focuses exclusively on males to avoid sex confounding. For the multi-site study, site effects are handled using ComBat harmonization method (neuroCombat package v1.0.13), with detailed before/after harmonization comparisons in Supplementary Tables 3a-b and Supplementary Fig 3. Motion-related confounds are addressed by including mean relative motion as a covariate in normative models and by excluding outlier volumes (framewise displacement >0.9mm). Additional confounders in mediation analysis are considered: sensitivity analyses were performed correcting for IQ (Supplementary Table 6), showing similar mediation estimates. The study acknowledges potential unmeasured confounders in the Discussion.
cr7_handling_of_confounding_variables.supporting_text: For each between-network rsFC (FCi), normative trajectories were modeled with Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) for the training dataset using the mgcv package v1.8 -42 (Wood, 2011). To model possible non-linear trajectories, a smoothing function was applied to age (predictor)... Mean relative motion was included as a co-variate of no interest... To account for site effects, we employed the ComBat harmonization method (Supplementary Tables 3a-b; Supplementary Fig 3) with the neuroCombat package v1.0.13 (Fortin et al., 2018)... We performed sensitivity analyses correcting for IQ and observed similar mediation estimates (Supplementary Table 6).
